rows.label: Concept
rows.text: The Global Positioning System uses ≥ 4 satellites whose positions and times are known to compute a receiver's (x, y, z, t) by measuring signal travel times (d = c·Δt). The constellation orbits at ≈ 20,200 km with ≈ 12 h periods, and relativistic clock corrections of ~38 µs/day are essential to maintain metre-level accuracy.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Distance from delay: d = c × Δt
GPS speed: v = √(GM/r) (r ≈ 26,600 km)
GPS period: T = 2π√(r³/GM) ≈ 12 h sidereal

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ 'GPS signal carries your position from the satellite.' ✅ The satellite only sends its OWN position + time. YOUR receiver computes your position by triangulating delays.  ·  ❌ 'Three satellites suffice for full 3D positioning.' ✅ Three give (x,y,z) only if the clock is perfect; a fourth is required for a practical unknown clock offset.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: The fourth satellite is not for redundancy — it solves the unknown receiver clock offset.  ·  GPS satellites are NOT geostationary; they sit in inclined medium Earth orbits.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Distance from delay: signal travel 0.07 s → distance = 3×10⁸ × 0.07 = 21,000 km.  ·  GPS speed: v = √(GM/r) at r ≈ 26,600 km from Earth's centre ≈ 3.87 km/s.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'GPS works by measuring signal strength.' ✅ It measures signal TRAVEL TIME (c × Δt), not strength.  ·  ❌ 'GPS satellites are geostationary.' ✅ They orbit at ≈ 20,200 km in inclined MEO orbits with ≈ 12 h periods — not geostationary.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Compute GPS satellite speed and period from its orbital radius.  ·  Explain the four-satellite requirement with unknowns.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Four satellites = four unknowns (x, y, z, t) — the key reasoning line.  ·  1 µs clock error ≈ 300 m of position error — instant conversion.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: A GPS satellite orbits at 20,200 km. Find its orbital speed and period.  ·  Why does a receiver need four satellites instead of three?

rows.label: Hints

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: GPS uses travel-time ranging from ≥ 4 satellites to fix (x, y, z, t).  ·  Satellite positions are computed from orbital mechanics (Kepler's laws).  ·  GPS satellites orbit at 20,200 km altitude with ~12 h periods.  ·  Relativistic corrections of ~38 µs/day keep clocks accurate.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: GPS fixes position by measuring radio signal travel time from ≥ 4 satellites.  ·  Four satellites allow solving the receiver clock error as a fourth unknown.  ·  GPS satellites orbit at ≈ 20,200 km in inclined MEO with ≈ 12 h periods.  ·  Relativistic corrections (~38 µs/day) are essential for metre-level accuracy.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: GPS was developed by the US Department of Defense and declared fully operational in 1995; it is freely available worldwide.  ·  The constellation was designed by military engineers using Newton's law and Kepler's equations — a textbook application of gravitational physics.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: If a GPS signal takes 65 ms to arrive, how far away is that satellite?  ·  Explain both special and general relativistic corrections to GPS clocks.  ·  Estimate the daily position error if all relativistic corrections were ignored.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: GPS orbit parameters (altitude, period) derive from satellite formulas — show the computation.  ·  Relativistic correction in GPS is a famous applied-physics question.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: GPS period ≈ 11 h 58 min (half a sidereal day).  ·  Clock offset: 1 µs error → position error ≈ 300 m.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: GPS determines a receiver's position by measuring: → B  ·  A GPS receiver needs at least how many satellites for a full fix? → C

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **What GPS is:** the Global Positioning System is a satellite-based navigation system that tells a receiver its exact 3D position on Earth. It uses the same gravitational/orbital physics as any satellite, which is why it lives in the gravitation chapter.  ·  **Principle of position fixing:** each GPS satellite broadcasts a radio signal stamped with its position and precise transmission time. The receiver measures the travel time of signals from at least four satellites and solves for (x, y, z, t) — the fourth equation corrects the receiver clock offset.  ·  **How distance is measured:** distance = speed of light × time delay. Since the receiver's clock is not atomic-precise, a fourth satellite provides the clock-error term, giving accuracy of a few metres.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Applications: navigation, timing, mapping, geodesy.  ·  Clock error mapping: Δposition = c × Δt_clock  ·  Relativistic shift: Δt ≈ 38 µs/day (GR +45 µs, SR −7 µs)

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: GPS relies directly on satellite motion physics (v = √(GM/r), T = 2π√(r³/GM)).  ·  ❌ 'Relativistic corrections are too tiny to matter.' ✅ Without them GPS would be off by ~10 km/day. The effect is 38 µs/day — essential.  ·  ❌ 'Position accuracy is limited by the number of satellites visible.' ✅ With ≥ 4 satellites you can fix position; more satellites reduce error statistics but don't change the basic math.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Relativity: 38 µs/day accumulated shift → ~10 km/day without correction.  ·  The relativistic effect: satellite clocks gain ~38 µs/day; compensation keeps GPS accurate.  ·  Error sources: ionosphere, multipath, clock drift, geometry (DOP).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: NEB asks conceptual questions about the working principle and the satellite orbit numbers.  ·  GPS needs ≥ 4 satellites to solve x, y, z and clock error simultaneously.  ·  Each satellite broadcasts its own position and precise time; the receiver does the compute.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: GPS orbit: altitude ≈ 20,200 km, period ≈ 12 h, speed ≈ 3.87 km/s.  ·  Relativistic corrections (~38 µs/day) are mandatory for GPS accuracy.  ·  Distance is derived from travel time (d = c·Δt), not from signal strength.
